title: One year of the Labour Codes: a checklist
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Five questions to ask a year after the Labour Codes took effect on 21 November 2025: rules, wages, social security, enforcement and BMS's concerns.
body:
The four Labour Codes came into force on **21 November 2025**. As their first anniversary approaches, it is a good moment to look at what has happened and what has not. Laws are tested by use, and a year is long enough to see which parts are working. This post offers a checklist of five questions that a worker, a union office-bearer or a State unit can ask, and gives, for each, what the public record shows as of early November 2026. We have drawn only on published sources and have said so where the record is thin.

## What was promised

When the Codes were announced, the Government described them as a modernisation of laws that largely dated from the 1930s to 1950s, consolidating 29 Central laws into four. The announced features included a national floor wage, minimum wages and timely payment for all workers, mandatory appointment letters, gratuity after one year for fixed-term employees, a single registration, licence and return, legal recognition of gig and platform workers with aggregator contributions, and an inspector-cum-facilitator system meant to guide employers as well as enforce the law ([Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/labour-codes-labour-laws-ministry-of-labour-central-govt-125112100754_1.html); [Labour Ministry release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf)). The Government also said that, during the transition, existing rules would continue where consistent with the Codes ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/01/03/labour-ministry-issued-faqs-on-the-labour-codes/)). The checklist below asks how far these promises have been turned into working arrangements.

## 1. Rules: have the Centre and your State framed and notified them?

**Centre.** The Labour Ministry pre-published draft rules on 31 December 2025, with 30 days for comments on the Industrial Relations Code and 45 days for the others ([The Week](https://www.theweek.in/wire-updates/business/2025/12/31/centre-pre-publishes-draft-rules-on-four-labour-codes-to-seek-stakeholders-feedback.html)). It notified the final Central rules on 8 and 9 May 2026, along with Model Standing Orders. These apply directly only where the Centre is the "appropriate Government" ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)).

**States.** The picture is uneven. An October 2026 law-firm newsletter lists States that have notified rules under the Industrial Relations Code (Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Lakshadweep, Rajasthan and Uttarakhand), and notes that the lists for the Wages, Social Security and OSH Codes are different ([ELB Newsletter, October 2026](https://www.amsshardul.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ELB-Newsletter-October-2026.pdf)). A tracker from May 2026 also showed many States still at the draft stage and warned readers to verify against official gazettes ([Lakshmikumaran & Sridharan](https://employmentlaw.lkslaw.com/rules)). On West Bengal, a Business Today report of 8 July 2026 said that the State had begun discussing implementation and was expected to start drafting rules ([Business Today](https://www.businesstoday.in/latest/economy/story/west-bengal-government-set-to-implement-labour-codes-541845-2026-07-08)). Please check the latest position with your State labour department.

## 2. Wages: has the floor wage been fixed, and has the minimum wage in your State been revised?

On the floor wage, the position as of mid-July 2026 was that the Government had begun setting up a 15-member Central Advisory Board and had not announced a timeline for notifying the National Floor Wage. The earlier non-statutory floor level was Rs 176 per day, last revised in 2017 ([Angel One](https://www.angelone.in/news/economy/government-initiates-national-floor-wage-exercise-with-advisory-board)). We have not found a notified floor wage figure in the sources we consulted. A May 2026 report added that the detailed minimum wage formula was dropped from the final Central wage rules, with the criteria to be specified separately by order, and that economists had warned this could lead to inconsistent wages across States ([Tradejini](https://www.tradejini.com/blogs/india-notifies-final-rules-for-labour-codes)).

Other wage ceilings have moved. On 17 September 2026 the Labour Ministry notified a rise in the EPF wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000 per month ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/09/19/labour-ministry-notifies-25000-wage-ceiling-under-social-security-code/)). BMS had asked earlier in 2026 for the ceiling to be raised to Rs 30,000, together with higher ESIC and Bonus Act ceilings ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/india/rss-affiliate-bms-flags-labour-code-implementation-gaps-seeks-5-day-week-for-banking-sector/2864682)). The newsletter cited above reports that, for the Bonus Act, the calculation ceiling is Rs 7,000 per month or the minimum wage, whichever is higher, and the eligibility ceiling is Rs 21,000. For your own checklist, compare your State's current minimum wage notification with your wage slip.

## 3. Social security: have schemes for gig, platform and unorganised workers been launched, and are aggregators contributing?

The architecture is in place. Under the Central Social Security rules of 8 May 2026, gig and platform workers aged 16 or above must register on a central portal, aggregators must share worker data within 45 days of the rules coming into force and then report new workers and exits, and a worker becomes eligible for benefits after at least 90 days of engagement with one aggregator, or 120 days across several, in the previous financial year ([ELB Newsletter](https://www.amsshardul.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ELB-Newsletter-October-2026.pdf)). On 1 June 2026 the Ministry directed online aggregators to complete linkage with the e-Shram portal by 21 June, and reported that 15 major aggregators, including Zomato, Swiggy, Uber, Ola and Rapido, had already joined ([SCC Online](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/06/02/eshram-deadline-aggregators-june-21-gig-workers/)).

States are acting as well. The same newsletter records that Telangana's Platform Based Gig Workers Act came into force on 2 June 2026, and that a Maharashtra bill on gig and platform workers was introduced on 3 July 2026. What we could not find, in the sources consulted, is public data on how many workers have actually received benefits, or how much aggregators have contributed. These are the numbers a union should ask for.

## 4. Enforcement: do inspectors respond, and is there a working facilitation system?

The Central rules push many compliance steps online. They provide for registration through the Shram Suvidha Portal with deemed registration after seven days, a single pan-India licence for contractors, and a rule that if a contract worker's grievance is not resolved by the principal employer's committee within 30 days, it must be forwarded electronically to the inspector-cum-facilitator ([Mondaq](https://www.mondaq.com/india/employee-rights-labour-relations/1807196/cracking-the-code-ii-the-new-central-labour-rules-at-a-glance)). A report on the final rules adds that a full-and-final settlement is to be cleared within two working days of separation ([Tradejini](https://www.tradejini.com/blogs/india-notifies-final-rules-for-labour-codes)). On paper, these are real improvements. Whether they work depends on the capacity of inspectors, the accessibility of the portals to workers without computers, and whether complaints get a response. A union can test this simply: file one complaint, record the date and track how long it takes.

## 5. Concerns: have the points raised about the IR and OSH Codes been discussed in tripartite meetings?

BMS's position has been consistent. In August 2025 its Central Executive asked the Government to roll out the Codes in phases, with consultation of the tripartite partners ([BMS press release](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=8936)). On 31 January 2026 it said it welcomed all four Codes, called the Wages and Social Security Codes historic and revolutionary, but raised concerns on the other two, and said it had raised these with the Labour Minister, who had assured it that they would be addressed ([BMS statement](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=9332)). On 25 February 2026 BMS held demonstrations in several States and submitted a memorandum seeking, among other things, universal implementation and resolution of worker concerns under the IR and OSH Codes ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/india/rss-affiliate-bms-flags-labour-code-implementation-gaps-seeks-5-day-week-for-banking-sector/2864682)). At its meeting in Ranchi on 26 to 28 July 2026, BMS decided to formally submit suggestions and objections on those two Codes ([Organiser](https://organiser.org/2026/07/29/372464/bharat/jharkhand-bms-national-working-committee-meeting-concludes-calls-for-eps-pension-hike-amendments-to-labour-codes/)).

Whether these points have been taken up in a tripartite forum is harder to say. The Indian Labour Conference, the main tripartite body, last met in July 2015, and a parliamentary committee asked in 2025 for it to be convened ([Business Standard](https://business-standard.com/india-news/house-panel-asks-labour-ministry-to-hold-labour-conference-at-earliest-125041800770_1.html)). We have not found a public record of such a discussion in the sources consulted, so this item remains open.

## What you can do

Write down your own experience. Did your employer give you an appointment letter in the new format, with the labour identification number and your Universal Account Number? Are wages paid on time, and are deductions within the 50 per cent cap? Is your provident fund and ESI in order, and do you know your UAN? If you work for an aggregator, are you registered on e-Shram? Note the answers, with dates and documents, and share them with your union. A union that gathers fifty such accounts from a district has a much stronger case than one that relies on impressions.

## Why a checklist

The first year shows what is working and what needs repair. Some parts, such as the digital registration and the e-Shram linkage, are visibly moving. Others, such as the floor wage and complete State rules, are still awaited. A balanced report card gives credit where it is due and presses where it is not.
